title: Press Note on Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) Monthly Bulletin September 2026
subtitle:
Urban labour force and workforce participation strengthened

Urban Female labour force participation reached highest level since October 2025

Overall UR remained stable, with a year-on-year decline
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                15 OCT 2026 4:00PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Snapshot:
Overall LFPR (15+ years) stood at 55.5% in September 2026, registering an increase of 0.2 percentage points over September 2025.
Urban LFPR (15+ years) increased to 50.7% in September 2026, up from 50.4% in August 2026.
Overall Female LFPR (15+ years) rose by 0.5 percentage points year-on-year to 34.6% in September 2026. Rural Female LFPR increased by 1.0 percentage point to 38.9% over the same period.
Overall WPR (15+ years) increased by 0.3 percentage points year-on-year to 52.7% in September 2026.
Overall UR (15+ years) remained stable at 5.0% in September 2026, down by 0.2 percentage points from September 2025.
Rural Female UR declined by 0.4 percentage points year-on-year to 3.9% in September 2026, the lowest level recorded during 2026.
A.        Introduction
The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), conducted by NSO, MoSPI, is the primary source of data on labour force participation and employment and unemployment conditions. The PLFS survey methodology has been modified from January, 2025 to provide monthly and quarterly estimates of labour force indicators for the country.
Monthly results of PLFS are released in the form of Monthly Bulletins. It presents estimates of key labour market indicators
viz.
Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR), Worker Population Ratio (WPR) and Unemployment Rate (UR) at the all-India level following the Current Weekly Status
[1]
(CWS) approach.
The Monthly Bulletins for April, 2025 to August, 2026 have already been released. The present Monthly Bulletin for September, 2026 is the eighteenth in the series.
Key findings for persons of age 15 years and above following CWS:
Rise in urban Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR):
The overall Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) for persons aged 15 years and above remained broadly stable at 55.5% in September, 2026, compared to 55.6% in August, 2026. In rural areas, LFPR was recorded at 58.0% against 58.2% in August, 2026, while the urban LFPR registered a moderate increase of 0.3 percentage points, rising from 50.4% in August, 2026 to 50.7% in September, 2026.
Over the year, the overall LFPR increased by 0.2 percentage points, from 55.3% in September, 2025 to 55.5% in September, 2026. During the same period, rural LFPR increased by 0.6 percentage points, from 57.4% to 58.0%, while urban LFPR registered a marginal decline of 0.2 percentage points, from 50.9% to 50.7%.
Urban LFPR showed a month-on-month improvement of 0.3 percentage points, reaching 50.7% in September, 2026.
Female Labour Force Participation gains momentum
in urban areas:
The overall female LFPR stood at 34.6% in September, 2026, compared with 34.8% in August, 2026. Urban female LFPR recorded a notable month-on-month increase of 0.5 percentage points, rising from 25.4% to 25.9% and reaching its highest level since October, 2025. Rural female LFPR estimated at 38.9% in September, 2026 against 39.4% in the previous month.
On a year-on-year basis, overall female LFPR increased by 0.5 percentage points, from 34.1% in September, 2025 to 34.6% in September, 2026. Rural female LFPR registered an increase of 1.0 percentage point, from 37.9% to 38.9%, while urban female LFPR remained broadly stable at around 26% (25.9% in September 2026, compared with 26.1% in previous year).
Rural female labour force participation registered a year-on-year increase of 1.0 percentage point, recorded at 38.9% in September, 2026.
Urban workforce participation strengthened
across genders:
The overall Worker Population Ratio (WPR) remained broadly stable at 52.7% in September, 2026, compared with 52.8% in August 2026. Urban WPR reached its highest level at 47.2% since October, 2025. This improvement was reflected across genders, with urban male WPR rising from 70.7% to 71.0% and urban female WPR increasing from 23.2% to 23.5%. Rural WPR moderated from 55.8% to 55.5% over the month.
On a year-on-year basis, overall WPR increased by 0.3 percentage points, from 52.4% in September, 2025 to 52.7% in September, 2026. Rural WPR recorded an increase of 0.7 percentage points, from 54.8% to 55.5%, while urban WPR remained broadly stable at around 47%. At the all-India level, male WPR rose by 0.4 percentage points to 73.6%, while female WPR increased by 0.5 percentage points to 32.8% over the same period.
Urban workforce participation strengthened across genders in September, 2026, with both male and female WPR rising by 0.3 percentage points, over the month.
Overall Unemployment Rate (UR) remained stable:
The overall Unemployment Rate (UR) among persons aged 15 years and above remained steady at 5.0% in September, 2026, compared with August, 2026. Rural UR remained broadly stable at 4.2%, against 4.1% in the previous month, while urban UR edged up marginally from 6.8% to 6.9%.
Compared with September, 2025, the overall UR declined by 0.2 percentage points and reached at 5.0% in September, 2026. Rural UR declined by 0.4 percentage points, from 4.6% in September, 2025 to 4.2% in September, 2026. UR in urban areas remained broadly stable from 6.8% in September, 2025 to 6.9% in September, 2026.
Rural UR recorded a year-on-year declined of 0.4 percentage points, reaching 4.2% in September, 2026
Unemployment Rate declined year-on-year for both male and female:
The overall male UR among persons aged 15 years and above remained stable at 4.9% in September, 2026 compared with the previous month, continuing the downward or stable trend observed since June, 2026. Urban male UR decreased from 6.1% in August, 2026 to 6.0% in September, 2026. Among female, the overall UR remained broadly stable at 5.2%, compared with 5.1% in the previous month. Rural female UR stood at 3.9%, its lowest level recorded during 2026, while urban female UR increased marginally from 8.9% to 9.2%.
A year-to-year comparison indicates that overall male UR declined by 0.2 percentage points to 4.9% in September, 2026, while overall female UR decreased by 0.3 percentage points over the same period. The decline was particularly evident in rural areas, where male UR decreased by 0.3 percentage points, from 4.7% to 4.4%, and female UR fell by 0.4 percentage points, from 4.3% to 3.9%.
Unemployment rates declined year-on-year for both genders, with rural female UR reaching its lowest level during 2026.

title: Ministry of Tribal Affairs holds the first meeting of the Working Group on Tribal Languages
subtitle:
Experts deliberate on a roadmap for documentation, digital preservation and promotion of tribal languages

Adi Vaani being positioned as the National Tribal Language Repository
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                15 OCT 2026 10:44AM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs held the first meeting of the Working Group on Tribal Languages today in a hybrid workshop mode. The meeting was chaired by Smt. Ranjana Chopra, Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs. Eminent linguists, academics, researchers and community language practitioners from across the country, including Padmashree Chamu Krishna Shastry, Chairman, Bhasha Samiti, and Dr. K. Sreenivasa Rao, former Secretary, Sahitya Akademi, participated in the meeting.
The Working Group was constituted by the Ministry with members from leading institutions, including the Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL), the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) at Delhi, Dharwad and Kanpur, Tezpur University, Manipur University, Assam University, Sikkim University, Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages, the Council for Diversity and Innovation (CoDIN) and the Bhasha Samiti, among others. The Working Group will guide efforts towards the documentation, preservation, research and promotion of tribal languages across the country.
Focus on Language Preservation and Community Participation:
Speaking at the meeting, Smt. Ranjana Chopra, Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, highlighted the importance of language in improving the outreach and effective delivery of welfare initiatives among tribal communities. She noted that Adi Vaani, which began as a translation tool for practitioners and administrators, has the potential to evolve into a comprehensive language repository bringing together corpora, primers, dictionaries and community stories. She also emphasised the importance of mother-tongue-based multilingual education in addressing learning gaps during the early years and called for bringing together the work already undertaken by institutions and scholars on a common platform, avoiding duplication of efforts.
Roadmap for Tribal Language Documentation:
Presenting the context of the initiative, the Joint Secretary highlighted the rich linguistic diversity of tribal communities and the need to document and preserve their languages. He outlined the proposed framework for the Working Group, covering a national baseline of tribal languages, research and scholarship, digital documentation and language technology, community-led documentation of oral traditions and cultural resources, multilingual education and learning materials, and partnerships among Tribal Research Institutes (TRIs), universities and other institutions.
Adi Vaani: Building a National Tribal Language Repository:
The meeting reviewed the progress of Adi Vaani, developed by IIT Delhi in collaboration with the Ministry. The platform offers text-to-text translation in nine tribal languages, along with speech, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and video subtitling features. It also provides searchable access to more than 300 primers prepared by TRIs. State TRIs have contributed approximately 13.9 lakh text sentences in ten languages and around 300 hours of speech data. The platform has recorded over 48,000 Android downloads and approximately 6,500 monthly users. IIT Delhi sought the Working Group’s support in linguistic validation of datasets, standardisation of spelling and orthography, and development of domain-specific vocabulary for planned pilots.
Seven Pillars for the Development of Indian Languages:
Padmashree Chamu Krishna Shastry, Chairman, Bhasha Samiti, outlined seven pillars essential for the development of any Indian language: sustained proficiency among speakers in their mother tongue; the use of language in education, administration, communication and entertainment; contemporary literature and knowledge content; continuous word generation to meet changing needs; adoption of technology; teaching-learning materials and systems, both online and offline; and support from Central and State Governments, corporates and society at large. He emphasised that speakers must remain at the centre of all language development efforts.
Recalling the words of the Hon’ble Prime Minister that all mother tongues of India are national languages, he stressed that no language should be considered small or big. He called for celebrating linguistic diversity in the spirit of
Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat
, where diversity is the beauty and unity is the strength, and encouraged a sense of closeness and mutual respect among speakers of different languages. He also suggested collaboration among the Bhasha Samiti, central and state tribal universities, the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR) and the IKS Division of the Ministry of Education, which has supported 38 tribal studies projects. He urged the Working Group to identify priority areas for focused action.
Plan for Documentation and Revitalisation:
Dr. K. Sreenivasa Rao, former Secretary, Sahitya Akademi, presented a plan for tribal language documentation and revitalisation. The proposals included state-wise and language-wise directories of writers, scholars and resources in a searchable national database; district-level community resource groups with trained tribal youth as researchers; revival of existing tribal language institutions; community digital archives hosted through Adi Vaani; and a two-year action plan with quarterly reviews. He emphasised that tribal communities should actively create and contribute to their own language resources as part of the vision of
Viksit Bharat
.
Institutional Collaboration and Language Technology:
Prof. Basavraj Kudagonti, Director, CIIL, Mysuru, suggested prioritising languages in phases, establishing region-wise teams with coordinators, and developing a common repository to which institutions and individual researchers could contribute. Prof. Shailendra Mohan, former Director, CIIL, highlighted the importance of a three-way partnership among communities, schools and universities, and proposed preparing an atlas of tribal languages and mother tongues across all States.
Dr. Karthick Narayanan, Executive Director, CoDIN, proposed a federated network of digital archives supported by common metadata standards, with Adi Vaani serving as the national gateway. He also offered CoDIN’s speech datasets and community training programmes to support the initiative.
Dr. Amalesh Gope of Tezpur University offered expertise in speech technology for tonal languages, along with dictionaries and speech datasets for languages of the North-East. Dr. Chaitra Puttaswamy of IIT Kanpur highlighted the importance of training community members in language documentation and using engaging, non-verbal prompts to develop parallel corpora. Dr. Monali Longmailai of Assam University shared her work on the community-based Bodo and Dimasa Heritage Digital Archive, while Dr. Samar Sinha of Sikkim University emphasised the need to develop technical vocabulary in tribal languages for school subjects and adopt language-planning approaches suited to smaller languages. Other members also shared their field experiences and offered institutional and technical support.
Integrating Tribal Languages into Education:
Representatives of the National Education Society for Tribal Students (NESTS) highlighted the potential of more than 525 Eklavya Model Residential Schools, serving over 1.7 lakh students, to use the platform in classrooms. They also noted that students, teachers and parents could contribute stories, poems and other content to enrich the national repository.
Concluding the meeting, Smt. Ranjana Chopra requested members to share details of the languages they have worked on and the resources available with them, so that these could be integrated into the platform in coordination with IIT Delhi. She stated that the Ministry would circulate the agenda items and prepare a roadmap for taking the work forward. She also emphasised that language resources developed with communities should continue to be owned by the communities.
The meeting marked an important step towards strengthening coordinated efforts for the documentation, digital preservation and promotion of tribal languages, with Adi Vaani envisioned as a national platform connecting linguistic research, technology, educational resources and community-led initiatives.

Interacting with a plethora of NSF heads, the Hon’ble Minister reiterated the need to work with further synergy to sustain India’s sporting excellence.
Dr. Mandaviya stressed that India needs a continuous pipeline of champions rather than relying on a handful of medal winners. “How long will Mirabai Chanu alone keep winning medals for us? We need to produce 10 more Mirabai Chanus. Every federation must take this responsibility seriously. We have to identify talent, provide the right training and create an environment in which athletes can progress to the highest level,” the Hon’ble Sports Minister said, underlining the need to identify and develop athletes who can sustain India’s medal-winning ambitions across sporting cycles.
Thursday’s NSFs conclave served as a review of India’s Asian Games 2026 performance and a platform to assess preparations for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, the 2030 Commonwealth Games and the 2030 Asian Games in Doha. It was attended by representatives from all major NSFs, including, shooting, athletics, boxing, archery, squash, wushu, and more.
Dr. Mandaviya also emphasised the need for more sports psychologists, sports science experts and high-performance mental trainers, to mitigate the loss of focus that athletes go through when competing on major international stages. He also urged every NSF to introduce more competitions, strengthen athlete preparation, work with dedicated commitment, as well as carry out honest assessment of gaps in performance and administration.
The conclave saw Shri Vineel Krishna, Joint Secretary (Khelo India), present a discussion on the convergence of Khelo India Scheme with NSFs, while Col. N.S. Johal, CEO (TOPS), gave a performance review of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games and the review of preparations for LA Olympics 2028. The revised Assistance to National Sports Federations (ANSF) guidelines booklet was also inaugurated at the conclave.
Minister of State for Youth Affairs and Sports Smt. Raksha Khadse called for all federations to align their work with the vision of the Khelo India Mission. “Every NSF must ensure that state and district-level federations are also in place and functioning effectively. This work has to be undertaken wholeheartedly, alongside talent identification. Identifying talent is only one part of the process; athletes must also receive the correct training and support to reach their potential,” Smt. Khadse said.
She stressed that NSFs must ensure that state and district-level federations are functioning effectively, alongside their responsibility for identifying talent. “Only through a collective effort can we strengthen athlete preparation, create a better pathway for talent and increase India’s medal tally,” she added.
Secretary (Sports) Shri Hari Ranjan Rao mentioned that India must aim to finish among the top three at the 2030 Asian Games in Doha, while the 2030 Commonwealth Games, which India is scheduled to host, should be treated as a major national challenge. “We have to strive to finish third at the Asian Games in Doha. For the 2030 Commonwealth Games, we must break our own record from the 2010 Commonwealth Games and finish among the top three. Since we are hosting the Games, every NSF must take the competition seriously and prepare accordingly. We must treat this as a challenge and work towards it from now,” he said.
Earlier, Shri Rao had described the sporting ecosystem as a four-tyre vehicle that could move forward only if all its components worked together: athletes, coaches, NSFs, and the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports along with the Sports Authority of India (SAI).

title: NITI Aayog’s Frontier Tech Hub Unveils Data Centre Evaluation Framework to Help States Plan for Sustainable Growth
subtitle: Framework aims to help States move from attracting data-centre investments to building investment-ready infrastructure, protecting critical resources and maximising long-term economic value
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                15 OCT 2026 3:55PM by PIB Delhi
content:
NITI Aayog’s Frontier Tech Hub has released the
Data Centre Evaluation Framework
on 14 October 2026 to help States plan for sustainable growth of data centres.
The release took place
in the presence of Prof. Abhay Karandikar, Member, NITI Aayog; Shri Anurag Jain, CEO, NITI Aayog; Ms Debjani Ghosh, Distinguished Fellow, NITI Aayog; representatives from the Ministry of Power, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the
Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)
, Ministry of Commerce; as well as representatives from industry and the media.
The Framework, developed with inputs from industry, MeitY, Ministry of Power and DPIIT, provides State governments with a practical approach to planning, evaluating and facilitating data-centre investments. It helps them assess infrastructure readiness, safeguard critical resources and maximise long-term economic and strategic value.
India’s data-centre capacity has grown from about 375 MW in 2020 to approximately 1.5 GW currently, driven by the growing demand for Artificial Intelligence (AI), cloud computing, high-performance computing and data-intensive digital applications.
As India accelerates its AI and digital transformation, data centres are emerging as critical infrastructure underpinning the country's technological and economic ambitions. While this presents a significant opportunity, data centres at increasing scale also place substantial demands on electricity, water, land, connectivity and local infrastructure. The focus therefore needs to move beyond attracting investment to ensuring that projects are developed in locations where the necessary infrastructure and resources can support them over the long term.
The Government of India has taken important steps to create an enabling environment for data-centre investments, including a tax holiday until 2047 for eligible foreign cloud service providers leveraging India-based data-centre infrastructure. As investments grow in scale, effective State-level planning and investment readiness will be critical to ensuring sustainable growth of the sector.
Speaking on the occasion, Prof. Abhay Karandikar, Member, NITI Aayog, highlighted the opportunity to leverage data-centre investments to build India’s technological capabilities. He emphasised the need to strengthen domestic R&D, industry–academia collaboration and Indian participation across the data-centre technology value chain. He also underscored the potential for India to develop innovative solutions in advanced cooling, energy efficiency and resource-efficient computing, converting infrastructure investments into long-term economic and technological value.
Shri Anurag Jain, CEO, NITI Aayog, highlighted the need to move beyond investment attraction towards investment readiness. He emphasised that States need to assess infrastructure availability, resource requirements and economic benefits before committing support to data-centre projects. The Framework provides a structured approach to help States make informed decisions, anticipate constraints and facilitate faster, more predictable project execution without creating an additional layer of regulation.
Ms Debjani Ghosh, Distinguished Fellow, NITI Aayog, highlighted, “As AI reshapes the global economy, data centres are becoming critical strategic infrastructure. For India, the opportunity is not simply to attract investment, but to build sustainable capacity that strengthens our competitiveness and delivers lasting economic value. This framework will help states make smarter decisions - identifying the right locations, planning infrastructure ahead of demand and ensuring that every investment creates measurable public value.”
A Framework for Investment-Ready and Sustainable Data Centre Growth
The Framework is structured around five pillars: Power and Energy; Water and Cooling; Siting and Environmental Sustainability; Economic and Strategic Value; and Policy, Governance and Implementation.
To ensure resource sustainability, key recommendations include assessing grid readiness and net grid draw, promoting renewable energy and storage-backed power, and evaluating basin-level water stress and public-supply impacts. The Framework also calls for rainwater harvesting, on-site water treatment and storage, and lifecycle plans for e-waste, batteries and other hazardous waste.
To maximise economic value, the Framework recommends identifying suitable data-centre zones, distinguishing colocation from active compute services, linking State incentives to measurable outcomes, and promoting
Make in India
across IT and non-IT infrastructure. These measures are supported by time-bound approvals, clear accountability and monitoring of project commitments.
The Framework is intended to serve as a decision-support tool for State governments, enabling them to evaluate investment proposals against infrastructure availability, environmental sustainability, economic value and implementation readiness. By identifying potential constraints early and providing greater clarity on project requirements, it seeks to improve investment decisions, reduce implementation risks and facilitate sustainable growth of India’s data-centre ecosystem.
The Framework seeks to help States plan better, move faster and convert the next wave of data-centre investment into sustainable capacity and lasting economic value.

title: Women, Work and Enterprise: India’s Push for Better Livelihoods
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                15 OCT 2026 12:23PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India’s women employment story is moving from participation to better-quality work. PLFS shows female Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) rising from 23.3% in 2017-18 to 40% in 2025, while Worker Population Rate (WPR) increased from 22% to 38.8%. Building on this improvement, policy support is strengthening women’s work through formal enterprise recognition, credit, market access, safer workplaces, skilling and new livelihood avenues. Now, the focus is on turning higher participation into stronger income, security and economic development.
Rising Women’s Employment and Expanding Economic Opportunities
Women’s employment in India is moving beyond presence alone. The
rise in labour force participation marks an important shift
, alongside greater focus on the nature and quality of employment.
As more women enter the labour force, the next dimension of progress lies in the opportunities that work creates.
Economic empowerment is strengthened when employment provides income, security, recognition and greater control over economic choices.
This broader transition is being supported through policies that expand women’s access to
safer workplaces, social protection, entrepreneurship, formalisation and financial opportunities
. These measures help strengthen the quality of women’s participation in the economy, translating into secure and empowering opportunities.
Quantity Shift: Rise in Workforce Participation
Women’s engagement with India’s labour market has strengthened considerably in recent years. For women aged 15 years and above,
LFPR increased
from
23.3% in 2017-18
to
40.0% in 2025
.
This increase has also translated into a larger share of women actually working.
WPR
increased from
22.0% for women in 2017-18 to 38.8% in 2025
. In absolute terms, an estimated
20 crore women aged 15 years and above were employed in India during 2025
.
Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR)
measures the share of the population that is either working or seeking or available for work.
Worker Population Ratio (WPR)
measures the proportion of employed persons in the population.
Women as Workers, Entrepreneurs and Economic Contributors
As participation expands, the nature of women’s engagement with the economy is also changing.
Women’s Growing Presence in Enterprise
An increasing number of women are taking up entrepreneurship and establishing their own businesses. Women’s entrepreneurship
broadens economic participation by creating opportunities to earn, build assets and grow businesses. It strengthens financial independence while expanding skills and access to resources.
Women-owned MSMEs:
As of October 2026,
~3.69 crore registered MSMEs
were women-owned,
representing ~
38% of all registrations.
Women in startups:
By March 2026, over
1.07 lakh recognised startups
had at least one-woman director or partner. These accounted for approximately
48% of all recognised startups
.
Women in Technology and High-Skill Sectors
Alongside entrepreneurship, women’s participation is also expanding across manufacturing and high-skill sectors.
As on July 2026, women constitute nearly
70% of the direct workforce
in mobile phone manufacturing. Across the wider electronics manufacturing sector, women account for nearly
30% of the workforce created over the last decade
.
Women are also building a significant presence in the semiconductor industry. They constitute around
25% of the workforce
and nearly a fourth of India’s chip design and engineering workforce (as on March 2025).
The civil aviation sector similarly reflects growing women’s participation in specialised roles. Women account for
15%
of pilots
in India, among the
highest
shares globally
.
Additionally, women account for
15% of air traffic controllers
,
11% of flight dispatchers
and
33% of Flight Operations Inspectors in DGCA
(as on June 2025).
The expansion is also visible in India’s research ecosystem. The
Research & Development Statistics 2025-26
report shows that women’s participation in STEM research careers increased from
13% in 2000-01 to 18.6% in 2020-21 and 29% in 2023-24
.
Building Women-Led Enterprises from Recognition to Growth
As women build businesses across different segments, support for their long-term growth becomes increasingly important. Formal recognition, finance and market access provide key areas for strengthening women-led enterprises.
Formalisation: Giving Women’s Work an Economic Identity
Many women-led economic activities begin at a small scale, making formal recognition important. Formalisation provides an official identity and improves access to credit, government schemes, skills and business development services.
Swavalambini Scheme (2025) :
The scheme supports young women from business ideation to enterprise creation through entrepreneurship training, finance and market guidance, and legal support. Selected participants also receive 21 weeks of mentorship and handholding to help develop sustainable enterprises.
It was launched in February 2025 as a pilot across
six
higher education institutions in Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Uttar Pradesh and Telangana.
The targets under the Swavalambini pilot have been achieved.
A total of
82 faculty members
had been trained under Faculty Development Programme;
1276 participants
have been trained out of 1200 participants under Entrepreneurship Awareness Programme; and
a total of
602 participants
have been trained out of 600 participants under Entrepreneurship Development Programme.
Yashasvini Campaign (2024)
: The campaign aims to promote greater participation of women in entrepreneurship by achieving
gender parity on the Udyam Registration Portal and Udyam Assist Platform by 2029
. It also seeks to promote the mandated
3% public procurement target for women-owned micro and small enterprises (MSEs).
It also supports existing and prospective women entrepreneurs through awareness, handholding and capacity-building initiatives.  As on
July 2026
, the Yashasvini Campaign had facilitated over
22 lakh women-owned MSME registrations.
Furthermore, in FY 2025-26, total procurement from women-owned MSEs was 3.8%, exceeding the 3% public procurement target.
Credit: Financing Enterprise Growth
Formalisation brings enterprises into the recognised business ecosystem, while
access to finance enables them to invest, innovate and expand
.
Financial Support for Women-led MSMEs
Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana (PMMY) : Launched in 2015
, PMMY seeks to expand access to collateral-free credit up to ₹20 lakh for micro and small enterprises engaged in non-corporate and non-farm income generating activities.
Since inception,
PMMY had sanctioned more than 57.79 crore loans by April 2026
, with women entrepreneurs accounting for
two-thirds
of all loans sanctioned.
Credit Guarantee Scheme for Micro and Small Enterprises:
The Scheme was launched to strengthen credit delivery to MSEs and improve access to finance for unserved and underserved entrepreneurs.  Under the Scheme,
women-led MSEs receive enhanced guarantee coverage of 90%, along with a 10% concession on the guarantee fee.
As on
February 2026
(FY 2000-01 to FY 2025-26)
,
it approved
~30.75 lakh guarantees
worth ~
₹2.07 lakh crore
for women-owned MSEs.
Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP):
The PMEGP is a
credit-linked subsidy scheme
that supports new micro-enterprises in the non-farm sector. Beneficiaries receive margin-money (subsidy) assistance against bank loans.   Under the Scheme, women are eligible for a
25% subsidy in urban areas and 35% in rural areas
.
By
May 2026
, women accounted for nearly
40% of all micro-enterprises assisted
under PMEGP. They also received around
45% of the total margin-money subsidy disbursed
.
Financial Support for Women-led Startups
Launched in
2016
,
Startup India
is the flagship Government of India initiative to promote innovation and build a strong startup ecosystem.
Under this, the Government supports
startups across sectors and at different stages of their business cycle through multiple funding initiatives.
Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS):
Established in
2016
, FFS
supports startup funding by providing capital to SEBI-registered Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs). In turn, AIFs invest in startups through equity and equity-linked instruments.
As of
January 2026
, supported AIFs have invested
~₹2,995 crore
in
women-led startups
from 2025 onwards.
Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS): Launched in 2021
, it provides seed funding to startups across sectors through approved incubators.
As of
January 2026,
incubators supported under the Scheme had approved
~₹294 crore
in funding for
women-led startups.
Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups (CGSS):
Operationalised from
April 2023
, CGSS supports collateral-free debt funding for eligible startups. It provides credit guarantees on loans extended by banks, financial institutions, NBFCs and SEBI-registered AIFs.
As on
January 2026
, loans amounting to
~₹39 crore
have been guaranteed to women-led startups.
Market Access: Connecting Women’s Work to Buyers
Market access helps women entrepreneurs reach more buyers and better understand demand, quality standards, branding and pricing.
Womaniya Initiative:
Womaniya is an
inclusion-focused initiative
on the Government e-Marketplace that connects women-owned MSEs and SHGs with formal government buyers. Through a dedicated digital interface, they can register and list products such as handloom, jute, coir and home décor items.
By July 2026
, over 2.17 lakh women-owned MSEs were registered on GeM
(a dedicated e-market for different goods & services procured by Government Organisations / Departments / PSUs)
.
In FY 2025-26, total contract value exceeded ₹28,000 crore to women MSEs, marking 27.6% growth over the previous year.
Women received 5.6% of the total order value awarded through GeM
, exceeding the mandated procurement target of 3%.
For detailed information, may refer to:
Womaniya: Building Inclusive Market Access for Women Entrepreneurs
Procurement & Marketing Support Scheme (PMS) :
The Scheme helps registered MSEs access markets through trade fairs, exhibitions, vendor-development programmes, e-commerce and packaging support.
Women-owned MSEs are eligible for a 100% subsidy
on built-up space rent for trade fairs.
MSME Trade Enablement & Marketing (TEAM) initiative :
To
provide MSE with access to digital marketing
, the TEAM initiative was launched for three years (2024-27) under the RAMP Programme. It aims to empower MSEs to access new markets, expand their customer base and boost income via
Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC).
Up till
2025-26
,
1,700 women-owned MSEs were registered
under the initiative.
Market access completes the enterprise value chain. Formalisation gives enterprises an identity, credit enables production, and market support turns production into income and sustainable growth.
Building the Skills Pipeline for Emerging Sectors
As women’s opportunities expand across technology and specialised sectors, future-ready skilling becomes important for widening access to these roles.

Launched in 2025,

aims to provide targeted skilling of 3,850 adolescent girls under PMKVY 4.0 in non-traditional and future-oriented job roles.  As of

.
AI Careers for Women
:
Launched in
2025
, the programme is
establishing 30 Centres of Excellence
in women's colleges across six states. These centres will
support 150 spoke centres
across Tier-II and Tier-III towns.
It aims to provide 20,000 learners with practical, industry-relevant AI training and project-based experience
. Participants will receive certifications, internships, apprenticeships, fellowships, career guidance and access to AI-enabled job opportunities.
Women in Science and Engineering–Knowledge Involvement in Research Advancement through Nurturing (WISE-KIRAN) :
The Scheme promotes women’s participation in science and technology R&D through fellowship and institutional programmes.
Fellowships include
WISE Fellowship for Ph.D. (WISE-PhD), WISE Post-Doctoral Fellowship (WISE-PDF), WISE–Societal Challenges with Opportunities (WISE-SCOPE), WISE Internship in Intellectual Property Rights (WISE-IPR) and Women’s Instinct for Developing and Ushering in Scientific Heights and Innovations (WIDUSHI).
These support doctoral and post-doctoral research, career re-entry, translational research, IPR training and continued research engagement.
Institutional programmes include
Consolidation of University Research for Innovation and Excellence (CURIE), Vigyan Jyoti, Gender Advancement for Transforming Institutions (GATI) and the Women in Space Leadership Programme (WiSLP)
.
In 2025-26,
180
women pursued PhDs,
606
women scientists received post-doctoral or translational research support,
26
senior scientists received R&D support, and
29,443
schoolgirls were supported in STEM.
More than
110
women scientists gained employment,
450+
saw research participation, skill upgradation or career re-entry.
These initiatives are strengthening women’s pathways into emerging and specialised fields through skilling and research support.
Labour Reforms Ensuring Safer Work Opportunities
For women, wider participation in the workforce depends not only on the availability of jobs, but also on whether those jobs can be accessed and sustained. Labour regulation plays an important role in shaping these conditions.
In November 2025, the Government
consolidated 29 existing labour laws into four Labour Codes
: the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code, Code on Social Security, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.
Within this consolidated framework, several provisions strengthen women’s workplace rights, safety, representation and access to employment.
Grievance representation:
Women must be represented in Grievance Redressal Committees in proportion to their workforce share.
Maternity benefits:
Eligible women receive up to
26 weeks of paid maternity leave
.
Adoptive and commissioning mothers
(a biological mother who uses surrogacy) are entitled to
12 weeks of maternity leave
. Other key provisions include:
Women are entitled to
₹3,500 as medical bonus
where free prenatal and postnatal care is not provided.
Women are entitled to
two nursing breaks
during the working day until the child is 15 months old.
Establishments with at least 50 workers must provide
crèche facilities.
The employer must allow four visits a day by the woman to the crèche which includes the rest intervals.
Wider work opportunities:
Women may work in all establishments, including night shifts with consent and prescribed safeguards.
Prohibition of Gender Discrimination:
Gender discrimination in recruitment, wages and employment conditions is prohibited.
Policy representation:
Women must constitute one-third of Central/ State Advisory Boards. The Board shall advice on minimum wages and measures to expand women’s employment.
Stronger Pathways for Women’s Work
India’s approach to women’s work is increasingly focused on strengthening the conditions in which women can
work and progress economically
. As opportunities widen, women’s contribution is becoming more visible across employment, entrepreneurship and newer areas of the economy.
Greater access to skills, finance, markets and enabling workplaces further supports these pathways.
This will deepen women’s role in India’s growth and advance women-led development on the journey towards Viksit Bharat.
